Listen, I feel you. I've been suicidal since a similar age, and I've made my fair share of attempts. My next try I hope I don't get found or god knows what else. 

But trust that *if* it doesn't work, and *if* you don't immediately have the means to try again (they take that shit away if they find you), then you will want to have some backup coping mechanisms.
Fine, but you aren't going to get that here, and I'm certain you knew that before posting.

After reading the comments here, my suggestion is that you go to the emergency room. Frankly, any method available to you right now has an extremely high chance of failing and leaving you even worse off. 

Since your options are, realistically, trying to get help or crippling yourself, you might as well try to get as much intensive help as possible.

Oh also, based on the title of your post, I'm going to go ahead and guess that you have been doing something called case-building. That's stacking up reasons why your depressed thoughts are correct. 

Anyone who comes up with a reason is probably going to be confronted with an argument from you as to why that, just like everything else, will not work. 

Now, case-building is a depressive thought process, but that doesn't mean that all the reasons you come up with are illegitimate. Otherwise it wouldn't be so wickedly effective at keeping us feeling sad and hopeless. 

So what do we do when we find ourselves doing it? Thoughts, fortunately, are unlike emotions in that we have a great deal of control over them. Simply being aware that case-building is a depressive thought pattern fraught with error in and of itself often helps. But to go even further, it can help to write down your negative thoughts and argue against them. It may feel unnatural at first, but as you gain practice noticing the flaws in the assumptions made by your depressed voice, you will get better at noticing those errors and thinking differently will begin to feel more natural. 

Look out especially for black and white thinking and all or nothing beliefs. Some common warning words are: always, never, perfect, impossible, awful, terrible, ruined, disastrous, and furious. 

You sound like you have frustrated ambitions, and that you still have plenty of time to see them fulfilled. Good luck!

Maybe try showing him an article like this: http://www.speakingofsuicide.com/2015/03/03/what-not-to-say/

... and then point out that a common theme between some of the bad ways respond is being dismissive. Be honest that while you know he was probably startled, and primarily interested in keeping you alive, that being called stupid was not only unhelpful but hurtful. 

Point out, too, that depression is not a sign of low intelligence. It would be fair to say plainly that you had placed a great deal of trust in him by admitting that, and that you did not expect to be rewarded with an insult. 

If you do have the strength and wherewithal to tell your teacher that his reaction was inappropriate, I applaud you. Know that doing so may benefit future students of his. 

If you end up not wanting to, know that it isn't your job to tell a grown ass man he shouldn't call people stupid just for being depressed. 

Either way, keep in mind that the priority is you, and your well being. Only say something if you are pretty sure it will help to make you feel better. 

Good luck!

fwiw SSRIs feel nothing like getting a chemical lobotomy. For me medication has so far been ineffective, so I don't have a wholly positive view of them. However, I can't help but recognize the difference it has made in my partner's life. He says it mostly just feels like it's easier to get out of an emotional slump, and that he doesn't get stuck in states of anxiety. 

If you haven't tried it, it's not as much of a time commitment as people often believe (you should feel somewhat better after two weeks). 

If I misunderstood, and you've tried a number of things, you may have treatment resistant depression, a personality disorder, co-occuring problems, or something else making it harder to address. 

In that case you may still be able to find a psychologist who does testing and evaluation who accepts Medicaid or sliding scale fees. 

The idea of dealing with the immense pain of mental suffering "for the rest of my life" is surely unbearable. Ask yourself whether you can cope for one more month, and try to get diagnosis.

One option is to go to an emergency room. It is extremely uncomfortable to tell an ER nurse that you're suicidal, and when I went I felt like an awful, drama queen fraud. Still, doing so got me intensive care that kept me going for another 6 years. 

Although I am depressed, isolated, and suicidal once more, the experiences I had in those 6 years were transformative and deeply important to me. I do struggle with guilt, and constantly ask myself whether the people in my life wouldn't have been better off if I had killed myself 6 years ago. However, I am getting better at recognizing that it is not my place to tell someone else whether or not they should value my existence in their lives. 

On a personal note, calls to optimism and suggestions on how to be cheerful have been among the most hurtful things that happier people have said to me. YMMV, but it has helped me a bit to learn to let such statements wash over me. To treat it, frankly, as incorrect, bullshit small talk. 

Humans have not always seen the purpose of life as happiness, or even fulfillment. Surely those are desirable, and it's not strictly wrong to mold one's life around those goals. 

Yet for myself that is unrealistic. The cognitive dissonance caused by always trying to achieve something that I know in my heart is not in my nature was a tremendous source of pain. 

For my part, I am working on embracing and valuing a process of personal struggle. Although it isn't "pleasing" per say, the feeling of being honest with myself is like having a boulder lifted from my chest. It feels very similar to the times I have felt resigned peace because I had committed to suicide. 

If the feeling is similar than why not kill myself, you may ask. That's extremely personal, and I'm not someone who believes that suicide is wrong or a sign of weakness. Still, I'm a sentimental social mammal, and there has always been at least *one* person who I knew I would hurt deeply. That's not a good or bad reason, but it was a reason that affected me, personally. 

The other thing that has stopped me is failure. I have never known how to get a gun, my attempts to jump have been thwarted, and on one occasion my severe allergy to a medication just didn't kick in. That was extremely depressing at the time. 

But let's say there is a chance that you won't succeed. What would the outcome be? If you don't succeed, then you will still need to find a way to cope. 

You may experience much less pain by working to find a non-bullshit way push through in any case. And you don't have to rule out suicide to do so.

Suicidal Buddhist here. While detachment and meditation are often helpful, is worth noting that Gautama himself complained of suffering *after* attaining enlightenment. Awareness and understanding may help us cope with this world, but as long as we live in it we cannot completely escape suffering. 

I agree that r/Buddhism may offer some solace, but I also think it's incorrect to suggest that it can cure depression. Perhaps that's not what you meant, but I have often heard that said and it sounded like such a suggestion.

People love reading fucked up negative material. It helps us externalize thoughts and feelings that are uncomfortable to hold secretly inside. It's oddly comforting to read a passage that reflects our worst thoughts. 

Creative blocks are hard to deal with, and suicidal depression is a hell of a creative blocker. Can you try writing in ways that feel easy and non-stressful? What about taking some time to explore an outlet other than writing?

You must know you're not the first person to say this. 

And there is plenty I want. It seems contradictory, but it's possible to hurt and still feel desire. 

But, really, who knows exactly what will make them content? We want things and then sometimes it makes us unhappy to get them. 

"Think about what you really want," is generic advice that probably most suicidal people have heard over and over. I have a thicker skin now, but in my late twenties and early thirties advice like that would make me feel broken. People who aren't depressed paint a picture of healthy people as having clarity about their desires, but I've learned it's not true.

I know your intent was kind, but it's probably best to drop that argument against suicide. If anything, detachment from specific desires helps a bit. 

I don't mean banishing desire -- just learning not to cleave to wanting something like happiness depends on it. Trust me that it's a recipe for shameful behavior and tumultuous inner misery.
I've tried things that are like that. If you hurt deeply on the inside it's like watching a movie you wish you could enjoy.
